questions.q: Which of the following is something a real SBOM records for each component, beyond just a package name?
options: The exact version, supplier, license, a package URL identifier, and its dependency relationships to other components
The developer's personal git commit history for that package
The salary cost of maintaining that dependency
A guaranteed list of every future vulnerability that will ever affect it
questions.explain: A real SBOM entry includes exact version, origin/supplier, license, a unique identifier like a package URL, and relationships showing which component pulled in which transitive dependency.

questions.q: Does an SBOM by itself tell you whether a listed component is currently vulnerable?
options: Yes, every SBOM entry includes a live vulnerability verdict
No — an SBOM is an inventory, not a scan result; a separate tool like grype checks the listed components against vulnerability databases
Yes, but only for components published in the last 30 days
No, because SBOMs never include version numbers
questions.explain: An SBOM tells you what's in a build, not whether it's dangerous. That judgment comes from feeding the SBOM into a vulnerability scanner such as grype, which matches each component's package URL against vulnerability data.

questions.q: What is the key difference in origin between the SPDX and CycloneDX SBOM formats?
options: SPDX only supports Python packages, and CycloneDX only supports JavaScript packages
CycloneDX cannot be generated by any open-source tool, only commercial ones
SPDX originated as a license-compliance format and became an ISO/IEC standard; CycloneDX, from OWASP, was designed security-first with native vulnerability-data support
SPDX is a newer format than CycloneDX and will eventually replace it
questions.explain: Both formats are real and in active use — SPDX grew out of license tracking and is now an ISO/IEC standard, while CycloneDX was built by OWASP specifically with security and vulnerability data as first-class concerns. Tools like syft can emit either.

questions.q: What does a package URL (purl) like pkg:pypi/requests@2.31.0 provide that a plain package name doesn't?
options: It encrypts the dependency so attackers cannot read its source
It automatically upgrades the package to the latest version on every scan
It replaces the need for a license field in the SBOM entry
A standardized, unambiguous identifier that vulnerability-matching tools can use to look up exactly that package and version
questions.explain: A purl pins the ecosystem, package name, and exact version in one standardized string, so a scanner like grype can match it precisely against vulnerability databases instead of guessing from a loose name.

questions.q: Why does having an SBOM generated ahead of time matter when a vulnerability disclosure affecting a widely used library comes out?
options: It lets you query whether any build's SBOM contains that package at the affected version, in minutes, instead of manually grepping lockfiles across every repository under time pressure
It automatically patches the vulnerable dependency without any human involvement
It prevents the vulnerability from ever being disclosed publicly
SBOMs are only useful for license audits and have no role in vulnerability response
questions.explain: Without a pre-generated SBOM, answering "are we affected" means manually checking lockfiles across every repo, likely missing transitive dependencies. With SBOMs already generated and stored centrally, it's a fast query against known package URLs and versions.
